Types of Machining Burrs Why Machining Burrs Matter Burr Removal Methods Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops Preventing Burrs in Machining Conclusion FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs CNC Machining Burrs (Envato) If you've ever run your hand across a freshly machined part and felt a sharp edge catch your skin, you've met the enemy: the burr. At first glance, it looks like a tiny flaw, but in machining, burrs are more than just a cosmetic annoyance. They can cut into assembly time, drive up costs, and in worst cases, create safety hazards for anyone handling the part. So, what is burr in machining? Think of it as the unwanted leftovers of the cutting process, those ragged edges, thin slivers, or raised ridges that show up after material is sheared, drilled, or milled. They're a headache for engineers and machinists alike because a part that isn't properly deburred can jam in an assembly, fail under stress, or even injure a technician. This is exactly why burr control matters so much in precision work. At JLCCNC, we've seen how burr-sensitive projects can make or break production runs, which is why we put the same focus on edge quality as we do on tolerances. And since our copper, steel, and aluminum machining starts at just $1 per part, even small shops can outsource tricky jobs and get parts that are both precise and safe to handle. What is Burr in Machining? (science direct) In machining, a burr is that unwanted bit of extra material left clinging to a part after a cutting process. Technically, it forms when the tool pushes or tears the material instead of slicing it away cleanly. What you get is a raised edge, a thin flap, or a tiny jagged lip that wasn't part of your CAD model, but now it's there, and it needs to be dealt with. You'll usually spot machining burrs around the usual suspects: along sharp edges, inside drilled holes, at the end of slots, or even wrapped around threads. Basically, anywhere the tool exits the cut is prime real estate for burr formation. Some are barely noticeable, while others can be sharp enough to slice a glove open or mess up an assembly fit. And here's the worst part: burrs aren't just a surface-level nuisance. They can ruin dimensional accuracy and surface quality, which is why deburring is almost always a required step in precision work. If you've read our guide on CNC Machining Surface Roughness: A Practical Guide , you'll know surface finish and edge quality often go hand in hand, burrs are just another part of that same equation. Types of Machining Burrs Not all burrs look the same, and knowing the type helps figure out the right removal method. Here's a quick breakdown of the most common machining burrs you'll run into: Burr Type Where It Shows Up What's Going On Poisson Burrs Along edges when cutting ductile metals Caused by plastic deformation pushing material sideways Roll-over Burrs Milling, drilling, and slotting operations Tool exit leaves a curled flap of material Breakout Burrs Exit side of drilled holes Material tears instead of shearing cleanly Cut-off Burrs Lathe parting or cut-off operations Extra material left behind as the tool separates the part Each of these has its own headache factor. A tiny Poisson burr might just ruin surface finish, while a chunky roll-over burr can jam an assembly or cut your hand open. Why Machining Burrs Matter (Intechopen) It's tempting to think burrs are just cosmetic, but they can cause problems way beyond looks. Here's why they matter: Impact Area How Burrs Affect It Assembly Tolerances Even a small burr can stop parts from fitting together cleanly Fatigue Life Burrs act as stress risers, shortening the lifespan of a component Safety Sharp burr edges can injure operators or end-users Post-Processing Costs Extra deburring steps = more time and money spent In high-stakes industries, one slip is all it takes. A single machining burr can cause part rejection in aerospace or medical applications, where safety margins are razor thin. And even outside of those fields, no customer wants a “finished” part that looks unfinished. Burr Removal Methods The method to remove burrs in CNC machining depends on part geometry, material, and how clean you need the finish. Here's a quick tour of the main approaches: Manual Deburring The old-school way: hand files, scrapers, sandpaper, or wire brushes. Cheap and flexible, but slow, and not consistent for production runs. Mechanical Methods Techniques like vibratory tumbling or grinding wheels are common in shops that need to batch-finish lots of smaller parts. Good for smoothing edges, but not always precise. Thermal Deburring Also called “explosive deburring.” Parts go in a sealed chamber, a gas mix is ignited, and burrs are literally burned off. Works well for internal burrs in tricky spots, but it's not the friendliest process for every material. Electrochemical Deburring This method uses an electrolyte and electric current to dissolve burrs in tight places<dynamic-value> cross-drilled holes or hydraulic components. Precise, but requires careful setup. Automated Deburring with Burr Machines This is where modern shops lean in. A burr machine uses abrasive brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to remove burrs automatically. The result: faster turnaround, less operator fatigue, and a more consistent finish. Method Pros Cons Traditional (manual / mechanical) Low entry cost, flexible for odd parts Labor intensive, inconsistent, time-consuming Automated (burr machines) High speed, repeatable results, great for production Higher upfront cost, needs proper setup Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops When people talk about shop efficiency today, burr machines and burr removal machines almost always come up. These systems combine abrasive heads, rotary tools, or even CNC attachments to take deburring from a bottleneck into a smooth step of the workflow. Machine Feature What It Does Why It Matters Abrasive Brushes Sweep away burrs on edges and surfaces Leaves a consistent finish without heavy labor Rotary Tools Target burrs in slots, grooves, or small features Great for complex part geometries CNC Integrated Deburring Toolpaths include deburring passes Saves setup time and reduces manual handling Benefits at a glance: faster cycle times, repeatable quality, and fewer operator hours spent hunched over a vise with a file. At JLCCNC , we've integrated advanced deburring directly into our workflow. That means when you send us burr-sensitive jobs, you're not just getting clean tolerances, you're getting parts that are ready to assemble straight out of the box. And with services starting at just $1/part, it's a no-brainer to let the machines (and our team) do the heavy lifting. Get a free quote today ! Preventing Burrs in Machining It's always cheaper and easier to stop burrs from forming than to spend hours removing them later. A few shop-floor best practices go a long way: Dial in tool geometry, feeds, and speeds → Sharp cutters with the right rake angle can slice cleanly instead of smearing the material. Running too slow or too shallow usually means burr city. Solid workholding → If a part vibrates or shifts even slightly, you'll see burrs at exit points. Lock it down, keep it stable. Coatings and coolants → TiN-coated tools paired with a proper cutting fluid help reduce adhesion and chip welding, both of which cause nasty edges. Design with burrs in mind → Chamfers, proper hole spacing, and avoiding thin unsupported features can dramatically reduce burr-prone zones. Conclusion Burrs might look like minor defects, but they stack up into real headaches, extra finishing costs, tolerance issues, safety risks, and sometimes full-on part rejection. The fix isn't just deburring afterward; it's knowing when to prevent burrs at the source and when to bring in the right burr machine for the cleanup. At JLCCNC , we've got both ends covered: precision machining that minimizes burr formation and automated deburring to handle the rest. The result is parts that are production-ready, safer, and more reliable. And with services starting at just $1 per component , outsourcing burr-sensitive jobs has never been simpler. FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs What is burr in machining? A burr in machining is a small, unwanted ridge or sharp edge left behind when material deforms or tears instead of cutting cleanly. How are machining burrs formed? They usually form at tool exit points<dynamic-value> hole edges, slots, or parting lines, when chips don't break away cleanly. What machine removes burrs? A burr removal machine uses brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to clean up edges quickly and consistently. Is deburring always necessary in CNC machining? Not always, but in industries like aerospace, automotive, and medical, deburring is non-negotiable for safety, fit, and reliability. What industries need strict burr control? Aerospace, medical device manufacturing, automotive, and electronics are big ones, anywhere a sharp edge or stray burr could compromise function or safety. Published Jan 02, 2024, updated Sep 28, 2026 10 min Table of Contents Waste Types and Where They Come From How to Measure Waste Reduction Lever 1: Design Optimization Lever 2: Material Management Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) Lever 4: Tool Maintenance Lever 5: Waste Recycling How to Prioritize These Five Levers What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste FAQ Need Help Applying This to Your Part? How to Reduce Waste in CNC Machining: 5 Practical Strategies Quick Answer: CNC machining waste is reduced mainly through DFM, near-net stock, efficient toolpaths, preventive tool maintenance, and alloy-segregated recycling. The biggest gains usually come before cutting: reduce unnecessary material removal and prevent scrap or rework. Every CNC-machined part starts as more material than it ends up being. A pocket gets milled out, a profile gets cut away, a boss gets faced down to size — and all of that removed material becomes waste, whether it's chips piling up in a bin or a block of expensive titanium reduced mostly to scrap. On some parts, the finished component is a small fraction of the raw stock's weight. Reducing that gap — without sacrificing the tolerances and finish a part actually needs — is less about any single trick and more about a handful of decisions made at different stages of the process, each with its own leverage. This guide covers the five main levers that actually move the needle on CNC machining waste, with links to deeper guides on the ones that have enough depth to warrant their own dedicated articles. Waste Types and Where They Come From Waste in CNC machining isn't one thing — treating it as a single category makes it hard to know what to fix first. It splits into four distinct types, each with a different cause and a different fix: Waste type What it is Mainly addressed by Unavoidable chips Material removed as part of normal subtractive machining — the literal byproduct of cutting a shape from solid stock Can't be eliminated, only recovered (Lever 5) Avoidable excess stock Material bought or left in the design beyond what the part actually needs — oversized billet, unnecessary wall thickness, stock faced away for no functional reason Levers 1 and 2 (design and material management) Scrap and rework Parts that fail to meet spec, or that require reworking, due to tolerance drift, poor finish, or tool-related defects Levers 3 and 4 (toolpath planning and tool maintenance) Spent tooling and coolant Worn cutting tools and used cutting fluid, treated as consumables but recoverable to a degree Lever 5 (recycling and reconditioning) Some of this is close to unavoidable — chips are the literal byproduct of subtractive machining — and some is genuinely reducible through better decisions upstream of the actual cutting. The five levers below map onto the "mainly addressed by" column above. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How to Measure Waste Reduction Before comparing levers, it helps to have a way to tell whether any of this is actually working. Three metrics cover most of it: Material utilization rate = finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight. This is the clearest single number for how much of what you bought ended up in the part versus the chip bin. Scrap / rework rate = number of parts scrapped or reworked ÷ total parts produced. Tracks the second waste type in the table above — quality-driven waste rather than design-driven waste. Alloy-segregated recycling recovery rate = value or weight of chips recovered by alloy type ÷ total chip volume generated. Reflects how much of the unavoidable chip waste is actually being recovered rather than landfilled or sold as low-value mixed scrap. Tracking these turns "reduce waste" from a general goal into something a shop can actually measure improvement against. Lever 1: Design Optimization The cheapest waste to eliminate is the waste that never gets created in the first place, and design decisions made before a part ever reaches the machine have the biggest leverage on that. A part designed with excessive material where it isn't structurally needed gets machined down to size anyway — every bit of that unnecessary material becomes scrap. Reviewing a design specifically for material efficiency (not over-specifying wall thickness "to be safe," not adding stock that gets faced away for no functional reason) catches waste before it's ever cut. Our design for manufacturability guide covers this kind of review in more depth, including the broader set of DFM considerations beyond just material efficiency. Lever 2: Material Management How raw stock gets purchased, sized, and — where relevant — nested against a part's actual dimensions has a real effect on waste before machining even starts. Buying near-net-shape stock (raw material close to the finished part's dimensions) rather than machining a small part from an oversized block cuts waste dramatically on parts where that option exists. Nesting specifically applies to sheet or plate stock and multi-part jobs — arranging multiple part outlines efficiently across a sheet to minimize the material lost between parts. It isn't a general CNC billet concept; a single part machined from a solid block doesn't have a "nesting" decision to make the way a batch of flat-pattern parts cut from a sheet does. Material choice itself matters too, but the substitution logic has to run in the right order: the material still has to meet the part's performance requirements first. Only once a shortlist of materials clears that bar does it make sense to compare them on available billet sizes, how predictably each machines at the removal rates the job needs, and what the resulting chips are worth as segregated scrap. Swapping to a "more machinable" alloy that doesn't meet the part's actual requirements isn't a waste-reduction win. Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) How the cutting itself is planned affects both direct material waste and the indirect waste from tool wear and rework. Efficient toolpath strategy — appropriate stepover, sensible roughing-to-finishing sequencing, avoiding unnecessary air-cutting or redundant passes — reduces both cycle time and the material removed less efficiently than it needs to be. Our guide on 5 CNC techniques to reduce waste in metal fabrication covers specific, actionable strategies at this level — smarter nesting, better blank sizing, intelligent toolpaths, optimized speeds, and simulation to catch problems before they become scrap. Lever 4: Tool Maintenance A dulling tool doesn't just cut less efficiently — it increases the risk of a part drifting out of tolerance or developing a poor surface finish, both of which can turn a nearly-finished part into scrap. Tracking tool wear against expected tool life, rather than running tools until they visibly fail, catches this before it produces bad parts. Our guide on tool wear detection and maintenance covers how to monitor this systematically rather than reactively. Lever 5: Waste Recycling What can't be avoided can often still be recovered. Metal chips have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled rather than landfilled — and for shops running enough volume, chip segregation by alloy meaningfully increases what that scrap is worth. Cutting fluid and coolant, often treated as a simple consumable, can be filtered, reconditioned, and reused rather than fully replaced on a fixed schedule. Our guide on zero-waste CNC strategies for recycling metal chips and coolant covers this specific piece of the waste picture — the recovery and recycling side, as distinct from the upstream prevention covered by the other four levers above. How to Prioritize These Five Levers Not every shop needs to tackle all five levers at once, and they aren't equally cheap to act on. A reasonable order to work through them: Check whether the billet or process itself can change first. Near-net-shape stock and process selection (Lever 2) are usually the single biggest lever available before any design or toolpath work happens. Then check whether the design is over-machining. A DFM review (Lever 1) catches unnecessary material and oversized stock allowances that would otherwise get machined away regardless of how efficient the toolpath is. Then reduce scrap and rework. Toolpath planning and tool maintenance (Levers 3 and 4) address the waste that comes from parts failing spec or requiring rework, which is often more expensive per part than raw material waste. Recover what's left. Recycling (Lever 5) is the last step because it deals with waste that's already unavoidable — chips and spent coolant that remain even after the first four levers are optimized. This order roughly matches how much control each lever has upstream of the actual cutting — the earlier a decision happens in this list, the more waste it prevents rather than merely recovers. What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste Treating waste reduction as purely a sustainability or compliance concern, separate from cost, undersells how directly it affects the bottom line. Every gram of scrap material is raw material that was purchased and then paid for again in machine time to remove — waste reduction is a cost optimization lever as much as an environmental one, and in most shops, the cost argument is what actually drives adoption. That said, waste reduction has a real failure mode worth naming directly: don't loosen functional tolerances, skip a necessary finishing pass, or lower a genuine quality requirement in the name of cutting material or cycle time. A part that comes back out of tolerance or fails in service because a step was cut to save material isn't a waste-reduction win — it's scrap with extra steps, and it usually costs more than the material it was meant to save. The "over-correcting" version of this mistake — tightening tolerances or adding excessive finishing passes in the name of "getting it right the first time" — is its mirror image, and can increase machining time and tool wear enough to offset whatever material savings were gained. Waste reduction works best as a set of deliberate, evaluated decisions at each of the five levers above — not a blanket instinct to cut corners, in either direction, everywhere at once. FAQ What percentage of raw material typically becomes waste in CNC machining? It varies enormously by part geometry, so there's no single figure worth quoting — a part machined from a mostly-solid block retains far more of the starting material than one with extensive pocketing or a complex profile cut from stock. The material utilization rate (finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight) is a more useful way to track this for a specific part than any general percentage. Does reducing machining waste affect part quality? Not when done correctly — design optimization, better material sizing, and efficient toolpaths reduce waste without compromising the part's function. The risk is over-correcting in either direction (see the section above), where waste-reduction efforts start affecting tolerance or finish negatively, or excessive caution offsets the material savings gained. Is scrap metal from CNC machining actually recyclable? Yes — metal chips and offcuts have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled, particularly when segregated by alloy type rather than mixed together, which affects the scrap's resale value. What's the easiest place to start reducing CNC machining waste? Design review and material/stock selection tend to have the highest leverage relative to effort — catching unnecessary material or oversized stock allowances before a part is ever machined avoids waste that's much harder to recover once cutting has already happened. Need Help Applying This to Your Part? Need to reduce material removal or rework risk before production? Upload your CAD model and include material, quantity, critical tolerances, and finish requirements for a manufacturability-focused quote review. Every JLCCNC quote includes a DFM check, the same review covered in our design for manufacturing guide — so waste-related issues get flagged before a part is cut, not after. Published Jan 02, 2024, updated Sep 28, 2026 10 min Table of Contents Waste Types and Where They Come From How to Measure Waste Reduction Lever 1: Design Optimization Lever 2: Material Management Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) Lever 4: Tool Maintenance Lever 5: Waste Recycling How to Prioritize These Five Levers What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste FAQ Need Help Applying This to Your Part? How to Reduce Waste in CNC Machining: 5 Practical Strategies Quick Answer: CNC machining waste is reduced mainly through DFM, near-net stock, efficient toolpaths, preventive tool maintenance, and alloy-segregated recycling. The biggest gains usually come before cutting: reduce unnecessary material removal and prevent scrap or rework. Every CNC-machined part starts as more material than it ends up being. A pocket gets milled out, a profile gets cut away, a boss gets faced down to size — and all of that removed material becomes waste, whether it's chips piling up in a bin or a block of expensive titanium reduced mostly to scrap. On some parts, the finished component is a small fraction of the raw stock's weight. Reducing that gap — without sacrificing the tolerances and finish a part actually needs — is less about any single trick and more about a handful of decisions made at different stages of the process, each with its own leverage. This guide covers the five main levers that actually move the needle on CNC machining waste, with links to deeper guides on the ones that have enough depth to warrant their own dedicated articles. Waste Types and Where They Come From Waste in CNC machining isn't one thing — treating it as a single category makes it hard to know what to fix first. It splits into four distinct types, each with a different cause and a different fix: Waste type What it is Mainly addressed by Unavoidable chips Material removed as part of normal subtractive machining — the literal byproduct of cutting a shape from solid stock Can't be eliminated, only recovered (Lever 5) Avoidable excess stock Material bought or left in the design beyond what the part actually needs — oversized billet, unnecessary wall thickness, stock faced away for no functional reason Levers 1 and 2 (design and material management) Scrap and rework Parts that fail to meet spec, or that require reworking, due to tolerance drift, poor finish, or tool-related defects Levers 3 and 4 (toolpath planning and tool maintenance) Spent tooling and coolant Worn cutting tools and used cutting fluid, treated as consumables but recoverable to a degree Lever 5 (recycling and reconditioning) Some of this is close to unavoidable — chips are the literal byproduct of subtractive machining — and some is genuinely reducible through better decisions upstream of the actual cutting. The five levers below map onto the "mainly addressed by" column above. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How to Measure Waste Reduction Before comparing levers, it helps to have a way to tell whether any of this is actually working. Three metrics cover most of it: Material utilization rate = finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight. This is the clearest single number for how much of what you bought ended up in the part versus the chip bin. Scrap / rework rate = number of parts scrapped or reworked ÷ total parts produced. Tracks the second waste type in the table above — quality-driven waste rather than design-driven waste. Alloy-segregated recycling recovery rate = value or weight of chips recovered by alloy type ÷ total chip volume generated. Reflects how much of the unavoidable chip waste is actually being recovered rather than landfilled or sold as low-value mixed scrap. Tracking these turns "reduce waste" from a general goal into something a shop can actually measure improvement against. Lever 1: Design Optimization The cheapest waste to eliminate is the waste that never gets created in the first place, and design decisions made before a part ever reaches the machine have the biggest leverage on that. A part designed with excessive material where it isn't structurally needed gets machined down to size anyway — every bit of that unnecessary material becomes scrap. Reviewing a design specifically for material efficiency (not over-specifying wall thickness "to be safe," not adding stock that gets faced away for no functional reason) catches waste before it's ever cut. Our design for manufacturability guide covers this kind of review in more depth, including the broader set of DFM considerations beyond just material efficiency. Lever 2: Material Management How raw stock gets purchased, sized, and — where relevant — nested against a part's actual dimensions has a real effect on waste before machining even starts. Buying near-net-shape stock (raw material close to the finished part's dimensions) rather than machining a small part from an oversized block cuts waste dramatically on parts where that option exists. Nesting specifically applies to sheet or plate stock and multi-part jobs — arranging multiple part outlines efficiently across a sheet to minimize the material lost between parts. It isn't a general CNC billet concept; a single part machined from a solid block doesn't have a "nesting" decision to make the way a batch of flat-pattern parts cut from a sheet does. Material choice itself matters too, but the substitution logic has to run in the right order: the material still has to meet the part's performance requirements first. Only once a shortlist of materials clears that bar does it make sense to compare them on available billet sizes, how predictably each machines at the removal rates the job needs, and what the resulting chips are worth as segregated scrap. Swapping to a "more machinable" alloy that doesn't meet the part's actual requirements isn't a waste-reduction win. Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) How the cutting itself is planned affects both direct material waste and the indirect waste from tool wear and rework. Efficient toolpath strategy — appropriate stepover, sensible roughing-to-finishing sequencing, avoiding unnecessary air-cutting or redundant passes — reduces both cycle time and the material removed less efficiently than it needs to be. Our guide on 5 CNC techniques to reduce waste in metal fabrication covers specific, actionable strategies at this level — smarter nesting, better blank sizing, intelligent toolpaths, optimized speeds, and simulation to catch problems before they become scrap. Lever 4: Tool Maintenance A dulling tool doesn't just cut less efficiently — it increases the risk of a part drifting out of tolerance or developing a poor surface finish, both of which can turn a nearly-finished part into scrap. Tracking tool wear against expected tool life, rather than running tools until they visibly fail, catches this before it produces bad parts. Our guide on tool wear detection and maintenance covers how to monitor this systematically rather than reactively. Lever 5: Waste Recycling What can't be avoided can often still be recovered. Metal chips have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled rather than landfilled — and for shops running enough volume, chip segregation by alloy meaningfully increases what that scrap is worth. Cutting fluid and coolant, often treated as a simple consumable, can be filtered, reconditioned, and reused rather than fully replaced on a fixed schedule. Our guide on zero-waste CNC strategies for recycling metal chips and coolant covers this specific piece of the waste picture — the recovery and recycling side, as distinct from the upstream prevention covered by the other four levers above. How to Prioritize These Five Levers Not every shop needs to tackle all five levers at once, and they aren't equally cheap to act on. A reasonable order to work through them: Check whether the billet or process itself can change first. Near-net-shape stock and process selection (Lever 2) are usually the single biggest lever available before any design or toolpath work happens. Then check whether the design is over-machining. A DFM review (Lever 1) catches unnecessary material and oversized stock allowances that would otherwise get machined away regardless of how efficient the toolpath is. Then reduce scrap and rework. Toolpath planning and tool maintenance (Levers 3 and 4) address the waste that comes from parts failing spec or requiring rework, which is often more expensive per part than raw material waste. Recover what's left. Recycling (Lever 5) is the last step because it deals with waste that's already unavoidable — chips and spent coolant that remain even after the first four levers are optimized. This order roughly matches how much control each lever has upstream of the actual cutting — the earlier a decision happens in this list, the more waste it prevents rather than merely recovers. What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste Treating waste reduction as purely a sustainability or compliance concern, separate from cost, undersells how directly it affects the bottom line. Every gram of scrap material is raw material that was purchased and then paid for again in machine time to remove — waste reduction is a cost optimization lever as much as an environmental one, and in most shops, the cost argument is what actually drives adoption. That said, waste reduction has a real failure mode worth naming directly: don't loosen functional tolerances, skip a necessary finishing pass, or lower a genuine quality requirement in the name of cutting material or cycle time. A part that comes back out of tolerance or fails in service because a step was cut to save material isn't a waste-reduction win — it's scrap with extra steps, and it usually costs more than the material it was meant to save. The "over-correcting" version of this mistake — tightening tolerances or adding excessive finishing passes in the name of "getting it right the first time" — is its mirror image, and can increase machining time and tool wear enough to offset whatever material savings were gained. Waste reduction works best as a set of deliberate, evaluated decisions at each of the five levers above — not a blanket instinct to cut corners, in either direction, everywhere at once. FAQ What percentage of raw material typically becomes waste in CNC machining? It varies enormously by part geometry, so there's no single figure worth quoting — a part machined from a mostly-solid block retains far more of the starting material than one with extensive pocketing or a complex profile cut from stock. The material utilization rate (finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight) is a more useful way to track this for a specific part than any general percentage. Does reducing machining waste affect part quality? Not when done correctly — design optimization, better material sizing, and efficient toolpaths reduce waste without compromising the part's function. The risk is over-correcting in either direction (see the section above), where waste-reduction efforts start affecting tolerance or finish negatively, or excessive caution offsets the material savings gained. Is scrap metal from CNC machining actually recyclable? Yes — metal chips and offcuts have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled, particularly when segregated by alloy type rather than mixed together, which affects the scrap's resale value. What's the easiest place to start reducing CNC machining waste? Design review and material/stock selection tend to have the highest leverage relative to effort — catching unnecessary material or oversized stock allowances before a part is ever machined avoids waste that's much harder to recover once cutting has already happened. (minaprem) If you've ever stood in front of a CNC machine or a manual lathe, you know that the cutting tool's geometry isn't just some arbitrary design. Every angle, edge, and surface has a job to do, and one of the most important of those is the rake angle . We've been running machines long enough to know that rake angle can make or break your surface finish, tool life, and machining efficiency. In this guide, we're going to walk you through what rake angle is, how it works, and how to choose the right one , without all the confusing textbook terms. The rake angle in a cutting tool is the angle between the tool\s rake face (the surface where the chip slides away) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. Think of it as how much your tool “leans” into or away from the cut: Positive rake angle: The Tool face leans forward toward the cut Negative rake angle: The Tool face leans backward away from the cut Why it matters: rake angle affects chip formation, cutting forces, tool wear, and even surface finish. Why Rake Angle is Critical in Machining (Istock) In real-world machining, even a small change in cutting tool rake angle can: Lower or increase cutting forces Improve or worsen surface finish Extend or shorten tool life Affect chip control and heat dissipation A good rake angle means the tool slices material efficiently. A poor one? It plows through the workpiece, causing chatter, heat, and early tool failure. A well-chosen rake angle can dramatically improve your part's surface finish. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. Final Thoughts Rake angle isn't just a textbook term, it's a real-world lever you can pull to make machining faster, cleaner, and more cost-effective. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. Final Thoughts Rake angle isn't just a textbook term, it's a real-world lever you can pull to make machining faster, cleaner, and more cost-effective. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: A Guide to Choosing the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Published Jan 27, 2024, updated Sep 15, 2026 18 min Table of Contents The Core Difference CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Decision Framework How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree Where Sheet Metal Wins Where CNC Machining Wins Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal One Hybrid Assembly Example Material Considerations The Real Cost Curve A Common Mistake Worth Flagging FAQ Not Sure Which Process Fits Your Part? Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: How to Choose the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Need CNC and Sheet Metal? We've Got Both JLCCNC does both CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication in-house. Upload your file, get an instant quote. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. A Common Mistake Worth Flagging Choosing a process based on which one a designer is more familiar with, rather than which one actually fits the part, is a frequent and costly habit. An engineer used to specifying machined parts sometimes defaults to CNC even for a simple bent bracket that sheet metal would produce at a fraction of the cost — not from any real requirement, just familiarity. Running through the decision factors and the 5-step tree above explicitly, rather than defaulting to habit, is a genuinely cheap way to avoid overpaying on a part that didn't need machining's capability in the first place. FAQ Is sheet metal fabrication always cheaper than CNC machining? Not always — at very low volume the two can be close, and for parts needing tight tolerances or complex 3D geometry, machining is often the only option regardless of cost. Sheet metal's cost advantage grows most clearly at moderate-to-high volume for parts within its geometric capability. Can a part be redesigned to use sheet metal instead of machining to save cost? Often, yes — if the part's function doesn't actually require variable thickness or fine 3D features, redesigning around uniform-thickness formed geometry can meaningfully cut cost, especially at volume. This is worth evaluating during design review rather than after tooling or a first production run. What tolerance can sheet metal fabrication achieve? Typical sheet metal tolerances run around ±0.1–0.3mm depending on the process and material thickness — tighter than many people assume, but still generally looser than CNC machining's ±0.01–0.05mm capability. Which process has a faster lead time? It depends on where you are in the product cycle. For a single prototype, CNC machining often turns around faster since there's no tooling or bend planning involved. Once you're ordering in batches, sheet metal generally catches up and can move faster per part, since cycle times on cutting and bending are short compared to machining time per unit. Do sheet metal and CNC machined parts ever get combined in one assembly? Yes, commonly — a sheet metal structure (enclosure, chassis) paired with CNC-machined components at the specific points needing tight tolerance is a standard approach, especially in electronics and equipment housings. Does material choice limit which process I can use? Not usually as a hard limit, but it changes the cost and quality picture. Softer, more formable alloys like 5052 aluminum favor sheet metal; harder alloys and stainless steel machine well but form less easily, and stainless in particular gets more expensive to machine due to work-hardening during cutting. Can sheet metal parts use threaded fasteners? Yes — without machining a thread into solid material. PEM self-clinching nuts, riveted nuts, and welded studs are the standard ways to add a threaded connection point to a sheet metal part, and they're usually cheaper than machining a thread would be on an equivalent solid section. When does stamping change the cost comparison? Stamping requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront tooling cost that only pays off at high volume — typically thousands of parts. Below that, laser cutting and press-brake bending (no tooling cost) is the more relevant sheet metal comparison against CNC, not stamping. Can sheet metal meet a ±0.05 mm requirement? Generally no, not directly out of the forming process — sheet metal tolerances typically run ±0.1–0.3mm. A feature genuinely needing ±0.05mm should be isolated to a CNC-machined component, even within an otherwise sheet-metal part or assembly. Note: tolerance and thickness figures throughout are typical ranges. Actual achievable tolerance depends on material, part size, and process — confirm against your specific part with an engineering review before finalizing a design. Not Sure Which Process Fits Your Part? Whether your part is a better fit for sheet metal or CNC machining often comes down to details that are easy to miss on a drawing alone — tolerance requirements, wall thickness consistency, or where your volume actually sits on the cost curve.
